title: Residence and source: who taxes what
summary: Countries tax on two bases: residence, which reaches a person's worldwide income, and source, which reaches income earned inside the country. Most cross-border tax problems start when both countries claim the same income.
body:
Bottom line. A country taxes its residents on everything they earn anywhere, and taxes non-residents only on income sourced in that country. Mr Shabazz, when you live in one country and earn in another, both can claim the same dollar, so your first two questions are always: where am I resident, and where was this income earned?

In plain English

Residence-based tax means a country taxes the people and companies that belong to it on their worldwide income. Canada does this. Under subsection 2(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), tax is payable on the taxable income of every person resident in Canada.

Source-based tax means a country taxes income that arises inside its borders, even when the person earning it lives elsewhere. Under subsection 2(3), non-residents are taxed in Canada on income from employment in Canada, a business carried on in Canada, and dispositions of what the Act calls taxable Canadian property, such as Canadian land. Passive payments to non-residents, like dividends and some interest, are usually taxed by withholding under Part XIII.

When a resident of one country earns income sourced in another, both countries may tax it. That is called double taxation. Foreign tax credits and tax treaties exist to reduce it.

The framework

Work through four steps.

  1. Find each person's residence. For an individual, Canada looks at factual residence: where you keep your home, your spouse or partner and dependants, and other ties such as bank accounts, a driver's licence and health coverage. The CRA explains its approach in Income Tax Folio S5-F1-C1, Determining an Individual's Residence Status. Under paragraph 250(1)(a), a person who sojourns in Canada for 183 days or more in a year can be deemed resident for that year. Companies follow the rules in lesson 25.
  2. Find the source of each income stream. Rent from land is usually sourced where the land is. Business profit is usually sourced where the business is carried on. Employment income is usually sourced where the work is physically done. Dividends are usually sourced where the paying company is resident.
  3. Check the other country's rules. Guyana sets its own residence and source rules and its own rates. Do not assume they mirror Canada's. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Find the relief. Canada may allow a foreign tax credit under section 126 for foreign tax paid on income Canada also taxes. A tax treaty, covered in lesson 34, may also limit one country's right to tax.

Two more points. Changing residence is itself a tax event. When an individual leaves Canada, section 128.1 generally treats him as having sold most of his property at fair market value, which is often called departure tax. And residence is decided on the facts, not by declaration: a statement that you are non-resident means nothing if your family and home remain here.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer lives in Alberta with his family and owns a rental building in Guyana personally. The building earns a hypothetical $100,000 of net rent a year.

Step 1: he is resident in Canada, so Canada taxes his worldwide income, including the Guyanese rent. Step 2: the rent is sourced in Guyana, because the land is there, so Guyana can tax it too, under its own rules for non-residents. Step 3: suppose Guyana takes a hypothetical $20,000. Step 4: Canada taxes the $100,000 at his personal rates, but may give a foreign tax credit for some or all of the $20,000, subject to limits in section 126.

Now suppose he moves to Guyana permanently with his family, sells his Alberta home and closes his Canadian ties. He becomes non-resident of Canada. Canada no longer taxes his Guyanese rent, but section 128.1 may treat him as selling certain property on departure, and Canada may still tax Canadian-source income, such as rent from any land he keeps in Alberta.

Professional Sign-Off Required: cross-border tax advisor (both countries)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is assuming that income earned abroad is taxed only abroad. A Canadian resident is taxed on worldwide income, and relief comes later through credits, not by exclusion. The second mistake is assuming that spending a few months away changes residence. Ties, not travel days alone, usually decide it.

How you will use it

As a developer working across borders, keep a simple residence and source table for yourself, your spouse and each entity. For each person or company, write the country of residence and the main facts that support it. For each income stream, write where it is sourced and which countries can tax it. Bring the table to your advisors in both countries at the same meeting, so neither plans in isolation. Before any move, any long stay abroad, or any change in where you live, ask for advice in advance, because residence changes can trigger tax on the day they happen. Keep a travel log of days in each country. It costs little and answers the question if anyone ever asks.
checklist: Write down the country of residence for yourself, your spouse and each entity
List the facts supporting each residence: home, family, ties
Record where each income stream is sourced
Note which countries can tax each stream
Ask how foreign tax credits apply before income is earned
Keep a travel log of days in each country
Get advice before any move or long stay abroad

selftest.q: You live in Alberta with your family but spend five months a year in Guyana supervising a project. Your Guyanese company pays you a management fee. Who can tax the fee?
selftest.a: You are very likely still resident in Canada because your home and family ties are here, so Canada can tax the fee as part of your worldwide income. Guyana may tax it as income sourced there, depending on where the work was done and its own rules. Canada may give a foreign tax credit for Guyanese tax, and a treaty, if one applies, may adjust the result.

apply: Make a two-column table listing each of your income streams and the country where each is sourced.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): subsections 2(1) and 2(3), paragraph 250(1)(a), section 126 and section 128.1. CRA Income Tax Folio S5-F1-C1. Guyana residence, source and rate rules are tagged unverified. Confirm current text with the CRA and with Guyanese advisors. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: cross-border tax advisor (both countries)

title: Tax treaties: what they do, tie-breakers, withholding
summary: A tax treaty is an agreement between two countries that decides which one may tax each kind of income, breaks ties when both claim the same person as resident, and caps withholding tax. It can only reduce tax that domestic law imposes; it does not create new tax.
body:
Bottom line. A tax treaty is a contract between two countries about who gets to tax what. Mr Shabazz, treaties reduce double tax by allocating taxing rights, breaking residence ties and capping withholding, but they only help if one actually exists between the two countries, you qualify for it, and you claim it properly.

In plain English

Two countries sign a tax convention, which is the formal name for a tax treaty. Each country then makes it part of its own law. In Canada, treaties are given effect by statutes passed by Parliament, and the Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act helps read them alongside the Income Tax Act.

Most treaties follow a template called the OECD Model Tax Convention, published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Each real treaty changes the template, so the article numbers and rates in your treaty may differ. Always read the actual treaty.

A treaty works mainly by limiting. It tells the source country to tax less, or not at all, and tells the residence country to relieve double tax. It does not create a tax that domestic law does not impose.

The framework

Using the OECD Model's numbering, the articles a developer meets most are these.

  1. Article 4, residence. If both countries treat an individual as resident, a tie-breaker applies in order: where the person has a permanent home, then where their centre of vital interests is, then their habitual abode, then nationality, and finally agreement between the two tax authorities. Companies have their own tie-breaker.
  2. Article 5, permanent establishment. A permanent establishment is a fixed place of business, such as an office or a construction site lasting longer than a set period. Under Article 7, a country can generally tax a foreign company's business profits only if they are attributable to a permanent establishment there.
  3. Article 6, income from land. The country where land is located keeps the right to tax income from it.
  4. Articles 10, 11 and 12, dividends, interest and royalties. These usually cap the source country's withholding at a lower rate than its domestic rate, often with conditions about ownership percentage or beneficial ownership.
  5. Article 13, capital gains. Gains on land, and often on shares that draw their value mainly from land, usually remain taxable where the land is.
  6. Article 23, relief. The residence country gives a credit or an exemption.
  7. Article 25, mutual agreement procedure. A route to ask both tax authorities to resolve double tax.

Then check three practical things:

  • Is there a treaty in force? Canada has a tax convention with Guyana, signed in the 1980s. Confirm it is in force and read its actual text and rates. [unverified — confirm independently]
  • Anti-abuse rules. Many treaties now include a principal purpose test, often added through the multilateral instrument, which denies a treaty benefit where obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement. [unverified — confirm independently]
  • Claiming the benefit. To get a reduced Canadian withholding rate, a non-resident usually gives the Canadian payer a declaration, such as CRA form NR301, before the payment. Other countries have their own forms.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical, and all rates are invented for illustration. A Guyanese project company pays a hypothetical $500,000 dividend to its Canadian holding company. Suppose Guyana's domestic withholding rate is a hypothetical 20 percent, and the treaty caps dividend withholding at a hypothetical 10 percent where the Canadian company owns a large enough share.

Without claiming the treaty, $100,000 is withheld. With a proper claim, $50,000 is withheld and $450,000 arrives. Canada then taxes the dividend under its own rules, which for a foreign affiliate depend on surplus accounts, covered in lesson 35.

Now a tie-breaker. The developer keeps a home in both Alberta and Georgetown. Both countries say he is resident. The treaty's first test, a permanent home, does not decide it because he has one in each. The second test, centre of vital interests, looks at family and economic ties. His spouse and children live in Alberta, so he is likely treated as resident in Canada for treaty purposes.

Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (both countries)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is assuming a treaty rate applies automatically. Usually the paperwork must be in place before the payment, and the recipient must meet every condition, including beneficial ownership. The second mistake is relying on the OECD template instead of the real treaty, whose terms can be very different.

How you will use it

As a developer, ask at the start of any cross-border plan: is there a treaty, which articles matter, and what forms and conditions are needed to use it? Get a copy of the actual treaty text from an official government source and keep it in your file. Make sure the holding company that receives the payments is the real beneficial owner and is resident where it says it is. Calendar the forms that must be filed before each payment. And never design a structure whose only purpose is to reach a treaty rate. Anti-abuse tests are aimed exactly at that.
checklist: Confirm a treaty exists between the two countries and is in force
Get the actual treaty text from an official government source
Identify the articles that apply to each income stream
Check ownership and beneficial ownership conditions for reduced rates
File the required declaration forms before each payment
Check for a principal purpose test or other anti-abuse rule
Use the mutual agreement procedure if double tax arises anyway

selftest.q: Your Guyanese company plans to pay its first dividend to your Canadian holding company next month. What should you do now to get any treaty-reduced withholding rate?
selftest.a: Confirm the treaty is in force and read the dividend article and its conditions, such as minimum ownership and beneficial ownership. Make sure the Canadian holding company qualifies and is the real beneficial owner. Provide whatever declaration or certificate the Guyanese authorities and payer require before the payment, and keep evidence of residence.

apply: Find and save an official copy of the tax treaty between Canada and any country you do business with, and note its dividend, interest and land articles.
sources: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, Articles 4, 5, 6, 7, 10 to 13, 23 and 25 (numbering in a real treaty may differ). Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act (Canada). CRA form NR301. The Canada–Guyana convention's status and rates, and any principal purpose test in it, are tagged unverified. All example rates are hypothetical. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (both countries)

title: Foreign affiliates: exempt and taxable surplus (concepts, sign-off required)
summary: When a Canadian company owns a foreign company, Canada tracks the foreign company's profits in surplus accounts that decide how much tax applies when dividends come home. Profits earned in the right kind of country can come home largely tax-free; others carry Canadian tax.
body:
Bottom line. Canada does not tax a foreign company's active profits when they are earned, but it watches them through surplus accounts. Mr Shabazz, whether a dividend from a foreign subsidiary comes home almost tax-free or carries Canadian tax depends on which account it comes from, and that depends partly on whether the foreign country has a tax treaty or information exchange agreement with Canada. This area always needs a specialist.

In plain English

A foreign affiliate is, broadly, a non-resident company in which a Canadian taxpayer owns at least 1 percent, and in which the taxpayer and related persons together own at least 10 percent. The definition is in subsection 95(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada). A controlled foreign affiliate is one that the Canadian taxpayer controls, alone or with certain others.

A surplus account is a running record, kept in Canadian tax terms, of the affiliate's earnings. The accounts are defined in section 5907 of the Income Tax Regulations. They exist only for Canadian tax; the foreign company's own books do not show them, which is why they must be tracked deliberately.

The framework

These are concepts only. The rules are among the most technical in Canadian tax.

  1. Exempt surplus. Broadly, active business income earned by an affiliate that is resident in, and carries on business in, a designated treaty country. A designated treaty country is generally one with which Canada has a tax treaty, or a tax information exchange agreement, in force. Dividends paid from exempt surplus to a Canadian corporation are generally fully deductible under paragraph 113(1)(a), so no Canadian corporate tax.
  2. Taxable surplus. Broadly, active income from countries that are not designated treaty countries, plus certain passive income. Dividends from taxable surplus are deductible only to the extent of underlying foreign tax, using a formula in paragraphs 113(1)(b) and (c). The rest is taxed in Canada.
  3. Other accounts. Hybrid surplus, mainly for certain gains on shares of other affiliates, and pre-acquisition surplus, which generally reduces the cost of the shares rather than being income.
  4. Ordering. Dividends are generally treated as coming first from exempt surplus, then hybrid, then taxable, then pre-acquisition, subject to elections. [unverified — confirm independently]
  5. FAPI. Foreign accrual property income is mainly passive income, such as interest, most rent and some service income, earned by a controlled foreign affiliate. Under section 91, it is taxed in Canada each year as it is earned, whether or not it is paid home. Holding passive investments abroad does not defer Canadian tax.
  6. Guyana's status. Whether Guyana is a designated treaty country, and from what date, must be confirmed. It affects whether a Guyanese affiliate's active income can be exempt surplus. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical, and all amounts and rates are invented for illustration. A Canadian holding company owns 100 percent of a foreign project company. Over three years, the foreign company earns a hypothetical $3,000,000 of active development profit, pays local tax, and keeps the rest.

Case A: the foreign country is a designated treaty country and the foreign company is resident there. The profit adds to exempt surplus. When a hypothetical $1,000,000 dividend is paid home, the Canadian company can generally deduct all of it. Only foreign withholding tax, if any, is lost on the way.

Case B: the country is not a designated treaty country. The same profit adds to taxable surplus. The Canadian company may deduct part of the dividend to reflect foreign tax already paid, and pays Canadian tax on the rest.

Case C: the foreign company instead invests its cash in bonds, earning interest. That interest is likely FAPI and is taxed in Canada every year, even if nothing is paid home.

Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (CPA or tax lawyer with foreign affiliate experience)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is not tracking the surplus accounts from the first year. Rebuilding years of Canadian-basis calculations later, from foreign books in another currency, is slow and expensive, and a dividend paid without knowing which account it comes from may cost more tax than necessary. The second mistake is letting a foreign subsidiary hold idle passive investments, expecting deferral. FAPI usually removes it.

How you will use it

As a developer with a foreign company, treat surplus tracking as part of the annual accounting, not a one-off. Ask your advisor to set up the accounts in the year the affiliate is acquired or formed, and to update them every year. Before any dividend, ask which account it will come from and what the Canadian tax will be. Keep the foreign company's surplus cash in its active business or send it home deliberately, rather than letting it earn passive income abroad. Canada also requires annual information returns for foreign affiliates, and the penalties for missing them can be significant, so add them to your compliance calendar. [unverified — confirm independently]
checklist: Confirm whether each foreign company is a foreign affiliate or controlled foreign affiliate
Confirm whether its country of residence is a designated treaty country
Set up surplus accounts in the first year and update them annually
Ask which surplus account a dividend comes from before paying it
Keep foreign surplus cash active or bring it home deliberately
Watch for passive income that could be foreign accrual property income
Add foreign affiliate information returns to the compliance calendar

selftest.q: Your Canadian company owns a foreign subsidiary that has earned active profits for five years, but nobody has tracked surplus accounts. You now want to pay a large dividend home. What should happen first?
selftest.a: An advisor should reconstruct the surplus accounts on a Canadian tax basis, confirm whether the country is a designated treaty country, and determine whether the dividend would come from exempt, taxable or other surplus. Only then can the Canadian tax be estimated and the dividend timed and sized. This needs specialist sign-off.

apply: For any foreign company you own, ask your accountant one question in writing: are its surplus accounts being tracked, and what is the current exempt surplus balance?
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): subsection 95(1) (foreign affiliate definitions), section 91 (FAPI) and section 113 (deduction for dividends from foreign affiliates). Income Tax Regulations, section 5907 (surplus definitions and designated treaty country). Dividend ordering, Guyana's designated treaty country status and foreign affiliate information return details are tagged unverified. All example amounts are hypothetical. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (CPA or tax lawyer with foreign affiliate experience)

title: Anti-avoidance: GAAR thinking and substance over form
summary: Canada's general anti-avoidance rule can deny a tax benefit from a transaction that follows the letter of the law but abuses its purpose. The best defence is a structure with a real business reason, real substance and documents that match what actually happens.
body:
Bottom line. Following the words of the tax law is not always enough. Mr Shabazz, the general anti-avoidance rule lets the CRA deny a tax benefit when a transaction was done mainly for tax reasons and defeats the purpose of the rules it relies on, so every structure should have a business reason you could explain to a judge without mentioning tax.

In plain English

The general anti-avoidance rule, usually called GAAR, is in section 245 of the Income Tax Act (Canada). It is general because it is not tied to any one transaction. It works like a safety net: when a plan technically complies with every specific rule but produces a result Parliament did not intend, GAAR lets the CRA deny the tax benefit.

A specific anti-avoidance rule targets one particular kind of planning, such as the shareholder loan rules or the attribution rules. GAAR sits behind all of them.

Substance over form is the idea that the real economic effect of a transaction matters, not just its legal labels. Canadian courts generally respect legal form. In Shell Canada Ltd v Canada, [1999] 3 SCR 622, the Supreme Court of Canada said that, absent a sham or a specific provision, legal relationships properly created should be respected. GAAR is one of the main exceptions to that respect.

The framework

Courts have applied GAAR as three questions, set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co v Canada, 2005 SCC 54.

  1. Is there a tax benefit? A reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax, or an increase in a refund.
  2. Is there an avoidance transaction? A transaction, or a series, that was undertaken primarily to obtain the tax benefit rather than for genuine non-tax purposes.
  3. Is it abusive? Does the result misuse a provision or abuse the Act as a whole, read according to its object, spirit and purpose? This is the hardest question. In Deans Knight Income Corp v Canada, 2023 SCC 16, the Supreme Court applied GAAR to a transaction that respected the words of a loss restriction rule but defeated its purpose.

Then three more points:

  • Recent amendments. Parliament amended GAAR in 2024. The changes are reported to lower the purpose test, add economic substance as a factor in the abuse analysis, and introduce a penalty in some cases. Confirm the current wording before relying on it. [unverified — confirm independently]
  • Sham. A sham is different from avoidance. It is where documents are meant to give a false impression of the parties' real arrangement. A sham is ignored entirely.
  • Other countries. Guyana and most countries have their own anti-avoidance rules, and treaties now often include anti-abuse tests. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer wants to move a hypothetical $2,000,000 of profit from an operating company to himself with less tax. An advisor proposes a series of share exchanges and redemptions through two new companies, each step allowed by a specific provision, that would produce a capital gain taxed at a lower effective rate instead of a dividend.

Ask the three questions. There is a tax benefit: the lower rate. The series appears to have no purpose except that benefit, since the developer controls every company before and after and nothing about the business changes. And the result may defeat rules that exist to tax corporate distributions as dividends, such as section 84.1, which is itself an anti-avoidance rule aimed at removing company surplus through share transfers between related people. A tax authority could argue the plan is abusive and assess the dividend tax plus interest and, under the amended rules, possibly a penalty.

Now compare a different plan. The developer brings in a new partner who buys shares for real money, and the company is reorganized to give the partner voting rights and financing obligations. Tax considerations shaped the design, but the transactions have a genuine commercial purpose and real economic effect. That is the kind of record that holds up.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and tax advisor (CPA)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is believing that every step being legal makes the whole plan safe. GAAR looks at the series and the result, not just each step. The second mistake is relying on an advisor's verbal assurance. Ask for written reasons, including the business purpose and an assessment of GAAR risk.

How you will use it

As a developer, apply a simple test to any structure: if you removed the tax saving, would you still do this, and could you explain why in one paragraph? If the answer is no, the structure carries GAAR risk. Write the business reason into the board minutes when the decision is made, not later. Make sure the documents match what actually happens: who decides, who takes risk, where money goes. Prefer structures whose tax result follows from real changes in ownership, financing or operations. And when an advisor presents a long chain of steps that changes nothing commercially, ask directly about GAAR, and ask for the answer in writing.
checklist: Write the non-tax business reason for every structure in the minutes
Ask whether you would still proceed if the tax saving disappeared
Check that documents match what actually happens in practice
Look at the whole series of transactions, not each step alone
Ask your advisor for a written GAAR risk assessment
Be wary of circular steps that change nothing commercially
Confirm the current wording of the amended GAAR before relying on any plan

selftest.q: An advisor proposes five steps, each allowed by a specific provision, that would let you take out company profit as a capital gain instead of a dividend. You will control every company before and after. What should worry you?
selftest.a: The plan appears to have no purpose except the tax benefit, and the result may defeat the purpose of rules that tax corporate distributions as dividends. Under the GAAR questions from Canada Trustco, there is a tax benefit, likely an avoidance transaction, and a real risk of abuse. Ask for a written analysis, including specific rules such as section 84.1, before proceeding.

apply: Pick one structure you use and write, in one paragraph, its business reason without mentioning tax. If you cannot, raise it with your advisor.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 245 (GAAR) and section 84.1. Canada Trustco Mortgage Co v Canada, 2005 SCC 54. Deans Knight Income Corp v Canada, 2023 SCC 16. Shell Canada Ltd v Canada, [1999] 3 SCR 622. The 2024 GAAR amendments and Guyana's anti-avoidance rules are tagged unverified. Read each decision before quoting it. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and tax advisor (CPA)
